text: Given an integer array, nums, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product, and return that product.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the subarray is contiguous and non-empty, values can be negative or zero, and the answer can itself be negative if that's the best?
Right. And every subarray product fits in a thirty-two-bit int.
Got it. Let me run through an example. Two, three, negative two, four — the best is two times three, which is six; the negative two would drag any product through it negative.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. This problem reminds me of Kadane's algorithm — the best subarray ending at i either extends the one ending at i minus one, or starts fresh at i. But products have a twist: a negative flips the largest into the smallest, and vice versa. So tracking only the max fails. On negative two, three, negative four, the answer twenty-four comes from the running min, negative six, times negative four. So I'll track both the max and the min ending at i, swapping them when the current number is negative.

Here's the plan. One: start the answer, max, and min all at the first number. Two: for each next number, if it's negative, swap max and min first. Three: max becomes the larger of max times the number and the number alone; min becomes the smaller; and the answer takes the max. One thing worth flagging — the swap goes before the multiply, and each update keeps a start-fresh-here option, the bare number. The answer starts at the first number, so all-negative inputs work. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it, and mention another approach if you have one.

The max-min tracking: one pass, three variables. The line that's easy to get wrong is where the swap sits — it has to happen before the multiply, so the old min becomes the base for the new max when the number is negative. And a slick alternative — prefix and suffix products, resetting on zero. A running product that hits zero restarts at one on the next step. Both are linear. One thing worth flagging — the best product is always a prefix or a suffix of a zero-free segment, so scanning both directions and resetting at zeros covers every case.

Let's dry-run the max-min version on three, negative two, negative three, four — expected seventy-two. The row that matters is the negative three: I swap first, so the running min, negative six, times negative three becomes eighteen — that's the negative-times-negative win only the min could catch. Then times four gives seventy-two. That matches. Corner cases: negative two, three, negative four returns twenty-four. A single negative number returns itself, thanks to the first-number init.

Time is linear, and space is constant, for both. Oh, one more thing — the whole difference from Kadane's maximum-sum version is the negative flip. Drop the multiply and you don't need the min or the swap at all. And if the task were the minimum product, I'd still track both, and just report the min of the answer and the min instead.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You tracked both max and min and swapped on negatives with the right ordering. You handled the restart-here term and the first-number init for all-negative inputs. And you gave the prefix-suffix alternative, plus the tie to Kadane. Good work.
